column5: revealed words placed on the heart
column6: The commentary says the taught word may be held in the heart as well as voiced. Deuteronomy commands that the words given that day be upon Israel's heart, making inward retention the first response to revelation.

column5: repeated words spoken through daily life
column6: The commentary treats recitation as an active oral practice. Deuteronomy tells Israel to repeat the words to children and speak of them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and on rising, giving memorized teaching a daily voice.

column5: teaching kept within and ready on lips
column6: The commentary's tongue-and-heart recitation has a close wisdom counterpart: Proverbs calls it pleasant to keep teachings within oneself when they are all ready upon one's lips.

column5: Torah within and written on heart
column6: The commentary's inward reading is more than quiet sound. Jeremiah's new-covenant promise places the Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, a strong Hebrew Bible image of internalized revelation.

column5: Arabic q-r-' label; Hebrew qara' book-reading
column6: The commentary labels 87:6 with q-r-'. Nehemiah uses Hebrew qara' for reading aloud from the Torah book and adds interpretation so that listeners understand, linking cognate reading to voiced instruction and comprehension.

column5: audible Scripture reading and understanding
column6: The commentary joins recitation with being aware of what is said. Philip hears the Ethiopian reading and asks whether he understands what he reads, a concrete Christian scene of oral scripture and understanding.

column5: Spirit-written letter on human hearts
column6: The commentary contrasts a text looked at with one retained in the heart. Paul calls the Corinthians Christ's letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than with ink, making inward inscription a reading-image.

column5: Spirit teaches and brings Jesus' words to remembrance
column6: The commentary reads 87:6 as divinely enabled recitation that does not forget. Jesus promises that the Spirit will teach and remind the disciples of his words, a direct Christian account of preserved taught speech.

column5: speak in hearts and be silent
column6: The commentary's first scene holds lowered voice beside interior speech. This psalm commands hearers to speak in their hearts upon their beds and be silent, a compact Hebrew pairing of inward utterance and silence.

column5: lips honor God while heart is distant
column6: The commentary permits remembrance with tongue and heart together. Isaiah critiques honor rendered with lips while the heart remains far away, adding the ethical test that exterior speech cannot replace inward attachment.

column5: lips and distant heart
column6: The commentary's two locations of worship are tested by Jesus' citation: these people honor God with lips while their heart is far from him. Its Christian use makes the tongue-heart relation a question of genuine worship.

column5: prayer and song with spirit and mind
column6: The commentary distinguishes raised sound from an inward mode of worship. Paul resolves a comparable pairing by praying and singing with both spirit and mind, bringing cognition into voiced prayer and song.

column5: calling on YHWH's name
column6: The commentary closes with remembering the Lord's name and prayer. Genesis describes people beginning to call on YHWH's name, an early biblical scene in which the divine name is invoked in worship.

column5: Hebrew zkr: God causes his name to be remembered
column6: The commentary's dhikr label links remembrance to the Lord's name. At the altar, YHWH promises to come where he causes his name to be remembered, using Hebrew zkr in a specifically cultic setting.

column5: Hebrew zekher, name, and desire of the soul
column6: The commentary's dhikr is possible in the heart as well as on the tongue. Isaiah joins God's name and zekher, "memorial/remembrance," to the desire of the soul, an inward cognate counterpart.

column5: YHWH exposes Sarah's inward laughter
column6: The commentary says God knows what is not openly voiced. YHWH questions Sarah's private laughter and its inner reasoning, giving a narrative instance in which concealed thought is directly known.

column5: prayer spoken in the heart
column6: The commentary allows divine address to remain inward. Abraham's servant says he had not finished speaking in his heart when Rebekah appeared, a prayer narrative that makes interior speech consequential before God.

column5: God alone knows every human heart
column6: The commentary joins prayer to divine knowledge of the hidden. Solomon asks God to hear from heaven because God alone knows the heart of every person, making omniscience part of temple prayer.

column5: deep counsel in the heart drawn out
column6: The commentary says a hidden thing can be extracted and illustrates it with water and a well. Proverbs likens purpose in a person's heart to deep water that one of understanding draws out, joining inner concealment and extraction.

column5: body made in secret not hidden from God
column6: The commentary moves from what is hidden to what God knows and brings into view. This psalm says a body made in secret in earth-like depths was not hidden from God, extending the claim to concealed organic formation.

column5: mouth uttering things hidden from the foundation
column6: The commentary connects recited speech with the disclosure of what lies hidden. Matthew presents Jesus' parabolic speech as uttering things hidden from the world's foundation, a Christian form of voiced unveiling.

column5: prayer to the Lord as knower of all hearts
column6: The commentary says inward realities are known to God. Before choosing Matthias, the disciples pray to the Lord specifically as the knower of everyone's heart, making the claim part of communal discernment.

column5: word judges thoughts and intentions of heart
column6: The commentary treats the recited word and hidden interior as joined under divine knowledge. Hebrews says God's word discerns thoughts and intentions of the heart, making spoken or written revelation an examiner of what is concealed.

column5: secrets of heart disclosed in worship
column6: The commentary connects hidden knowledge, audible word, and prayer. Paul says an outsider's heart-secrets are disclosed and that person then worships God and declares God's presence, a tightly related congregational scene.

column5: rain prepared for earth and grass made to grow
column6: The commentary explicitly imagines rain drawing pasture from soil. Psalm 147 says God prepares rain for the earth and makes grass sprout on mountains, matching rain, ground, growth, and divine agency in one verse.

column5: planting, watering, and God giving growth
column6: The commentary makes pasture's emergence God's act despite rain and soil. Paul distinguishes human planting and watering from God who gives the growth, a Christian agricultural image of the same agency distinction.

column5: voice heard from fire but no form seen
column6: The commentary locates loud and hidden speech beside Moses' fire and explores visible versus concealed. Deuteronomy says YHWH spoke from fire, Israel heard a sound of words, but saw no form, uniting auditory revelation with visual withholding.

column5: fire, dense darkness, and a great voice
column6: The commentary places loud speech, concealment, and the Moses-fire setting together. In WLC's Hebrew verse numbering, Deuteronomy recounts YHWH's great voice from fire, cloud, and dense darkness, an unusually close cluster of those images.

column5: brightness that Israel could not gaze at
column6: The commentary's secondary image is sight defeated by excessive light. Paul says Israel could not gaze at Moses' face because of its glory, making visual incapacity caused by radiance explicit.

column5: unheard voice without speech or words
column6: The commentary's phonetic scene contrasts audible high speech with what remains unspoken. Psalm 19 says there is no speech or words and no voice is heard, yet its surrounding hymn presents creation as communicating; the parallel is poetic rather than liturgical.

column5: few words before God
column6: The commentary invokes a measured rather than raised prayer-voice. Ecclesiastes warns against hasty speech before God and says that human words should be few, an explicit wisdom restraint on devotional utterance.

column5: Moses read while a veil lies on the heart
column6: The commentary connects reading, heart, and covering. Paul says that when Moses is read a veil lies on the heart, a Christian interpretive image in which scriptural reading itself can remain interiorly covered.

column5: mouth opened in parable and ancient dark sayings
column6: The commentary makes disclosure possible through a spoken word. The psalmist opens his mouth in a parable to utter ancient riddling sayings, a Hebrew example of voiced transmission of what is not immediately plain.

column5: liturgical remembrance in enacted worship
column6: The commentary joins dhikr to prayer. Paul's Eucharistic command, "do this in remembrance of me," makes remembrance a repeated Christian worship-act, though its object and rite differ from remembering God's name in 87:15.

column5: keep a king's secret; reveal God's works
column6: The commentary turns secret and open into a movement of disclosure. Tobit distinguishes keeping a ruler's secret from honoring God by revealing God's deeds, supplying a Jewish ethical rule about concealment and proclamation.

column5: earth produces first blade, then ear and grain
column6: The commentary's pasture comes out of the earth. Jesus describes the earth producing the crop in ordered stages beginning with the blade, a parabolic vegetal emergence whose setting differs from the commentary's rain image.

column5: well-mouth stone rolled away for watering
column6: The commentary gives a cleared well whose water is made visible as an image of disclosure. Genesis describes shepherds rolling the stone from a well's mouth to water sheep and replacing it, a concrete cover-and-uncover water scene.

column5: previously hidden things now announced
column6: The commentary says God may bring the hidden out. Isaiah tells the audience that hidden things they had not known are now announced, a prophetic disclosure formula rather than a physical emergence image.

column5: unapproachable light that no human can see
column6: The commentary says overwhelming light can function like a cover to sight. First Timothy places God in unapproachable light whom no human has seen or can see, a theological extension of visual excess beyond the sun-image.
